doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Writing 'Soulful Brother Gillespie' and hearing 'Slim Goody' on the subway
summary: Gardner turned the beat into a tune and big band chart, and recalls singing a melody into his answering machine after hearing it on the subway.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But I wrote an entire tune based off of that beat, and I called it “Soulful Brother Gillespie.” And I even expanded it into a big band arrangement. So that’s to say I’ve composed off of many influences, from something like that or I might hear the melody first. I wrote a tune on my first CD the title track is called “Slim Goody.” And I heard that melody while I was on the subway when I was living in New York, I was traveling on the subway to visit my girlfriend at the time. And it was before cell phones. And so I heard this melody in my head. But I was right in the middle of my journey uptown you know. And I said I can’t forget this melody. So I just started singing it to myself you know, and people started looking at me on the subway — nobody talks about anybody © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

strange on the subway. So when I got to my subway stop I went to a pay phone and called my answer machine and sang it into the answer machine so I wouldn’t forget it. Because you know you’ll think of something like at night when you go to sleep and your mind is open. And — man I really like that melody, okay, when I get up tomorrow I’m going to write it down. And you get up the next morning and say what was that thing I thought about last night, and it’s gone. You can’t even think about it.
